#6681. ‘We Just Are So Gagged’: Jordan Firstman and Reggie Absolom on Club Kid’s Success

The film’s stars discuss their excitement, their music tastes, and how they interpret that ending.

This story contains spoilers for Club Kid.

For his debut feature film, Club Kid, Jordan Firstman envisioned a curly-haired boy who could live in a world of adults. The story was well established by the time casting agent Carmen Cuba met British actor Reggie Absolom, who had appeared in Silo and other series. Firstman, who wrote, directed, and starred in the film, knew he was the perfect one to play Arlo, the 10-year-old son that Firstman’s character Peter never knew he had. Firstman and Absolom grew close quickly and developed a unique friendship that hasn’t slowed down post-filming. “We text all day,” Firstman says.

The pair spoke to ELLE about Reggie getting to DJ for the film, whether he’ll have a Radiohead phase, and what the movie says about family.

Jordan Firstman: I had a very extensive list of things I wanted in the character, and my casting director was like, “You really need to manage your expectations because you’re looking for a child actor. Baseline, you have to find someone good.” I also just wanted them to be naturally cool and not feel like a child actor [but] feel like a kid. I wanted them to have curly hair. I wanted them to look enough like me that they could be my kid. In the script, the character is written as half Indian, and she was like, “Babe, you’re just not going to find all of that.”

I found Reggie, and he checked every box. He looked like the kid I had in my head when I wrote it. He also was a really natural actor and nothing felt forced. I sent him a playlist of songs I wrote the movie to, and he told me which ones he liked. I thought he had really good taste, and we just talked for a while and got ice cream. And then it wasn’t until in the process that I found out he was a quarter Indian too. He literally had every single thing that I wanted, and so it did feel like a miracle in a lot of ways.

Reggie Absolom: It was a bit weird at first. But then I became such good friends with everyone anyway and it just felt like I fit in there. It didn’t matter how old I was. I was just friends with everyone, and I was just working like they were as well.

JF: I love sending people that I love music. Reggie’s music taste influenced the characters. He was into Slipknot at the time, so I wrote a little Slipknot into the script, and he also liked Massive Attack and Cocteau Twins, once I sent him my playlist. I wrote that in.

There’s this whole other component of the actual club music, on which we collaborated so closely with David Peck, who’s in the movie [and who wrote songs for the film and performed them as Heather Asylum]. He did Reggie’s whole DJ set and River Moon consulted. We had real DJs in the scene helping me and making sure we had all the right tracks. The music in the movie is everything; it’s the throughline in the story and the construction of the movie.

RA: You get most of the credit. You gave me quite a few songs, like Cocteau Twins ones and really good Massive Attack ones. I was like, okay, I’m going to go deeper into these and listen to all of their albums. Now there’s some songs that I would’ve never really listened to. When I listened to Cocteau Twins, I would’ve been like, “Okay, this is weird.” But now I’m like, “Okay, maybe I like the weird kind of songs.”

JF: I think you’re going to also have a major Radiohead era.

RA: Maybe, but I don’t know. I don’t like Radiohead.

JF: We were going to do “Maybe I’m Amazed” by Paul McCartney, and he wasn’t responding to our emails about licensing it. The day before [we filmed the scene], I was trying to think of other songs, and “Thoroughfare” is my favorite song, I think ever. I feel like I would be that dad that made my kid play Ethel Cain on the piano with me. Then we played it, and it felt really cute and really sincere. We still sang Paul McCartney, but they were like, “You don’t need Paul McCartney. Don’t waste your money.” And “Thoroughfare” is the vibe.

RA: It got me into a lot of different types of music, which I’m happy about. DJing was really fun and something that I’d want to do in the future. Maybe not a full-time job, but something on the side to do, something fun.

RA: It didn’t really influence the roles I wanted to get, but now that I’m in a film that’s done so well, it’s opened up for me to maybe get bigger roles than I would’ve expected before filming this.

RA: The idea of being in a movie, that was the next step for me. I was filming maybe three episodes of a series. I felt like no matter the role, just being in the movie would be the next thing to do. Then the fact that this was a lead role and that I felt similar to Arlo personality-wise in some ways. I felt like I could perform really naturally with the things that Arlo says and the way that he acts.

JF: Kramer vs. Kramer is such a classic and a movie I love. I often reference An Unmarried Woman with Jill Clayburgh. I love her relationship with her daughter in that movie and how they treat each other like adults. Because Peter has no experience with kids, he doesn’t know how to treat them like anything else but how he treats everyone.

JF: Once I started writing it, I started really understanding Peter and Arlo and what they needed. I actually feel like it’s a gift that they didn’t end up together for both of their lives for that time. That phone call [at the end] is so important, because the door opens again once they’re ready. I think it would’ve been too intense for Peter to [raise Arlo full-time]....He still wasn’t completely out of the party scene. He was still selling drugs. He was not ready to really do this in a real way. Arlo really needed a year of knowing true stability and a normal childhood.

But I think what Peter and his community offered Arlo was a very different version of normal. They encouraged creativity. For a traumatized kid, having an art practice is everything. In my darkest times as a kid, I turned to art. To me, it’s a very human ending, and to me it’s hopeful.

RA: Both of them needed to have that break. They’re trying to find themselves and what they should do. Now, another thing, whilst Arlo was with Peter, he was getting no education really. He tried to get him into school.

RA: He just gave up on that. The ending also leaves it up to interpretation what happens to them in the future. Obviously, it could have been like, oh, they rejoin and they’re father and son forever. I think it’s nicer when the film has an ending that’s up to interpretation a bit, where there could be different branches on the ending.

JF: He really enjoyed fatherhood, so I think he will continue his relationship with Arlo and help him through his teen years and grow up.

RA: In my opinion, Peter with a baby, adopting a baby would be a bit, like Edison says, “He’s all prepared. Forget the trauma,” or something like that.

RA: He could do it. He’d need Oscar [Peter’s partner, played by Diego Calva].

JF: No one involved in this project has had this happen to them. Even Cara [Delevingne] has never been a part of something like this. We just are so gagged. We can’t believe this is happening and that people are responding to it in this way. We get standing ovations everywhere we go, and it’s surreal. We don’t take for granted that this is a rare thing that happens.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6678. Glee Is Getting a Reboot Series 11 Years Later: Everything We Know So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Glee has always held a special place in Ryan Murphy’s heart, so when he heard the show was having a major resurgence on social media, it planted the seeds for a reboot in his mind.

“That show is interesting because it’s come back around,” he said in a July interview with People. “So many young people now watch it. And I’m like, ‘Maybe we should revisit that show.’ My nostalgia and love for that show is enough that I’m like, ‘Well, maybe people would like to see a new incarnation of that in some capacity.’ So yeah, I love that show, and I loved what it became and what it meant to so many people.”

Months later, Murphy delivered on his comments—on October 21, Disney+ and Hulu granted a series order for Glee, 17 years after the original show’s premiere and 11 years after the final episode. The series also announced the news on its official Instagram, writing, “It’s official. Glee is returning.”

Details about the reboot are currently sparse, but here’s everything we know so far.

Yes. In September, Murphy told Entertainment Tonight that there has been progress with writing the show. “We have a script. Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan], and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something,” he said.

The original cast of Glee included Lea Michele, Kevin McHale, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss, Jane Lynch, Amber Riley, Jenna Ushkowitz, Dianna Agron, Heather Morris, Matthew Morrison, Mark Salling, Jonathan Groff, Chord Overstreet, and Harry Shum Jr. Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera were also part of the original cast, but died in 2013 and 2020, respectively.

While Murphy did not state which stars he has been talking to, he told Entertainment Tonight that he’s “been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Hours after the reboot news was revealed, Variety reported that Michele will reportedly join the cast of the reboot. “She’s in,” a source told the outlet, while a second source added, “It’s still early-ish days, but it feels good and we’re happy to get the band back together.” Murphy and Michele did not provide a comment.

Following the news, Morris hinted that she’d be stepping back into Brittany S. Pierce’s cheerleading uniform. “Yes ladies and gentle men of women, rumors are true. Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years. But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well…and back for more #Glee,” she captioned a throwback photo of herself from the set.

While the post feels like a confirmation, Murphy has not confirmed any of the cast members who will return for the show.

Overstreet and McHale also hinted that they’d be returning. Overstreet wrote, “reunited and fit feels so good!” after the reboot news dropped. McHale reacted to a tweet that said Drake has surpassed the Glee cast with the most Billboard Hot 100 chart entries. “Challenge accepted,” he replied to the tweet.

On October 23, Deadline offered an update on Morris’s and Overstreet’s statuses. The outlet reported that they were in talks to join the reboot.

During his November 11 appearance on The Daily Beast’s Obsessed podcast, Colfer revealed that he’s planning to have more “conversations” about potentially joining the reboot.

He added, “It was really hard going back to the show after Cory passed, and I’m sure it’d be really difficult, especially now that Naya’s gone too,” Colfer said. “But I guess you have to think, are you going to let the loss of two people you love very much prevent you from being around a dozen other people you love as well? There’s a lot to think about with it.”

Colfer does have ideas on what his character, Kurt Hummel, would be up to in the current timeline, though. “I would love to see him like a Miranda Priestly-type, running his own fashion blog or a magazine,” he shared. “I could also see him on tour with Chappell Roan, styling her. There’s a lot of fun avenues they could explore.”

Over the years, several cast members have shared their reactions to a potential Glee reboot, with some stating they would not return to the series if it were made.

Michele, who played the show’s central main character, Rachel Berry, told E! News in September that she’d be open to following Murphy if he expanded the Glee universe. “I love Glee, I will always love Glee,” she said. “I love Ryan Murphy; it holds such a special place in my heart for me, so I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.”

Colfer told Bustle in an interview earlier this month that Glee “was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone.” He added, “I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no.”

Lynch reflected on her Glee character, Sue Sylvester, in an interview with Entertainment Tonight earlier this month and confirmed that she would join the cast again in a heartbeat. “I would be in like that,” she said.

In May 2025, Riley, who starred as Mercedes Jones, said that she wouldn’t be interested in returning to Glee during her appearance on Monét X Change’s Monét Talks podcast.

“I just feel like what we did was so phenomenal, I don’t want to risk trying to reinvent the wheel,” she said. “Now if they redo it, I think that’s amazing, because there are so many kids now that are just now discovering Glee, and so I think that that’d be really dope. But, you know, we lost cast members. I just feel like the chemistry, that formula, was so specific, and it’s changed now, so I don't know if it would be as effective. I’m always prepared for that question.”

Morris (Brittany S. Pierce) shared in a 2024 interview that she would be down to join the reboot if it were made. “I would,” she said in a video interview. “I think the film industry has come a long way. It was a really tough show to do, and I think being in the space that I’m [in] now, absolutely. I yearn so bad to be in a musical again.”

In 2023, Criss (Blaine Anderson) discussed a potential reboot and revealed that he would be on the fence about it.

“I’m not against it. I know people would like that. I think what made Glee so special is where it sat in its specific time and place,” he explained during his PeopleCon appearance. “I think a lot of cultural moments are defined by the alchemy of where we’re at as a society, and the way it called and responded to each other made it really special.”

Criss continued, “While I, as a fan of Glee, would go, ‘Yeah, I would love to see more,’ I do think there’s something we have to remember about the why, when, and how [the show was] special being very specific to one time. I wouldn’t be against it, but I’m also not screaming to do it. I’m somewhere in between. They have to make it really count.”

At AdoptTogether’s annual Los Angeles Baby Ball in 2022, Ushkowitz (Tina Cohen-Chang) told E! News that she would be open to a reboot if the right team worked together to bring it to life.

“If Ryan was doing it and the right people were involved,” she told the outlet at the time. “I would consider it.” She also dispelled rumors of drama between members of the cast, adding, “We’re a family—families don’t always have to get along. When we were working together, it took more energy to fight than it did to just get along. I spent more hours with them than literally, my own family.”

#6677. The Miami Heat Dropped Brand-New Jerseys Just in Time for Grand Theft Auto VI

Growing up in Oakland, Miami Heat forward Keshad Johnson and his brother Kenny used to sneak away from their parents to play Grand Theft Auto. “It caused some fights between me and him on turns,” Johnson says. “We used to play that if you crash the car, you gotta pass the sticks.”

For many of us who came of age in the early aughts, sneaking away from our parents to play GTA was a rite of passage. And since the first edition of the game dropped in 1997, at least part of the thrill of this fictional world was often tied to the clandestine affair. But next week, Johnson won’t be hiding from anybody. Instead, he’ll be part of a once-in-a-lifetime Grand Theft Auto experience when he and his Heat teammates take the court in special-edition Vice City jerseys inspired by the game.

Grand Theft Auto VI, Vice City, launches on November 19th. But the night before, when the Heat and superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo take on his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, they'll be ringing in what is by most accounts the biggest video game launch of all time with a special event that only Rockstar Games and the Heat could pull off. “My whole family is trying to get a Vice City jersey,” Johnson said when we spoke last weekend.

“We're bringing sports and entertainment together in a way that's never been done,” adds Miami Heat Chief Creative Officer Jennifer Alvarez. “And we're going to deliver an experience that no one has actually had at an NBA game.”

More on that in a second. But let’s start with the kits: all black, with bright pink accents that pop like neon signs in the South Beach sky. The word “Heat” is splashed across the front. “It's kind of like the outlaw type vibe,” Johnson said. “That's what we want to give when we're on the court.”

Hidden inside the letters and jersey numbers is a map of Miami streets. They were designed by Nike and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack, whose logos are featured on the jersey and shorts. As the whole campaign makes clear, details matter.

“I feel like Vice City has its own fashion culture,” says Heat star Bam Adebayo.

The jerseys will be available for purchase on game night at the arena, where fans will be transported into the video game itself upon entering the Kaseya Center, whose plaza will be made over with a Grotti Cheetah and Albany Manana, just two of the sports cars one can drive in GTA.

A sign hoisted atop the arena will read “Welcome to Vice City.” In fact, Mitchell was late to practice one day because his usual route was blocked by a helicopter that’d been deployed to help install it. “It shows how much time and effort they're trying to put into this new game,” Mitchell says. “This is probably gonna be the greatest game of all time.”

Though everyone involved has kept tight-lipped about what happens once inside the arena, fans attending Heat games have already been able to order burgers from Burger Shot and chicken from Cluckin' Bell, two fictional fast-food chains in the Grand Theft Auto universe. “It's a full 360 experience. I can't wait for people to really understand what that means,” Alvarez said, coyly. “And that's all I can say about it.”

One can understand the secrecy, since the Heat’s Vice City takeover has been two years in the making. It all started when Rockstar Games dropped the trailer for Vice City in December 2023. A digital Kaseya Center can be seen in the first 30 seconds.

“When we saw that we were in the trailer, we thought we should figure something out,” Alvarez recalls. “Because we've been synonymous with the word Vice since 2017."

The Heat launched the Miami Vice campaign in 2017 with its acclaimed Original Vice jerseys that set the standard for NBA teams launching City Edition jerseys. Those campaigns went beyond the uniforms and included local activations like custom license plates and a fashion line created in collaboration with local artists. Over the years, the Heat launched five separate Vice jerseys, each campaign expanding on previous ones. Ask those with the Heat, and they’d agree that this latest installment is the biggest one yet. “It feels like all of it built up to this,” Alvarez said.

To be clear, the Heat don’t look at this as an extension of their own Vice line. Rather, this is meant to be as exclusive as any streetwear brand launch. Also, it’s not easy to transport fans into a video game every single night. Go big, then go home.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has infiltrated Miami, turning the city that inspired Vice City into Vice City itself. Burger Shot came to life through a collaboration with Skinny Louie, a local smash-burger joint that has rebranded their brick-and-mortar (and arena) locations for the launch. Rockstar Games has activations throughout the city, including in Downtown, Little Haiti and the famous Wynwood Walls. It’s an Inception-style, video game outside the video game-type thing that crescendos with the Heat game on the eve of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch.

Players got their first look at the jerseys and the campaign during a team meeting in early October. After hours of presentations about business operations, media responsibilities and other team matters, the energy in the room sparked when Alvarez took the microphone and showed the first Vice City slide. The players locked in. A few even stood up and cheered.

Mitchell, for his part, was taken back to his childhood, when he would come home from his grandma’s house and play Grand Theft Auto until it was time for bed. For a while, Mitchell became obsessed, playing GTA while other popular games like Call of Duty and NBA 2K collected dust.

“I just played that all the time, doing missions, but also just running around,” he remembers. “It's kind of like your own world in a way.”

And next week, he’ll get to enter it IRL.

#6676. Phoebe Dynevor Gives a First Look at Her Wedding Ring—and It’s a Timeless Classic

Two months after her marriage to Cameron Fuller, Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring has finally been seen out on the town. The actor gave us our first glimpse of the stack on her ring finger while stepping out for coffee in London’s Notting Hill neighborhood—and it proved to be a true classic.

Since her wedding in France this August, Dynevor has worn a simple gold band paired below her gold solitaire oval engagement ring, which features a slender bezel setting. Rather than choosing a style embellished with micro-pavé gemstones or a large eternity ring wrapped with diamonds, the minimal band proves you can let the center stone of your engagement ring do the talking.

Just because the wedding band is simple doesn’t mean Dynevor’s stack is boring, though. Her oval-cut diamond likely sits around three carats, taking up some major real estate on the Bridgerton star’s slender finger. And while the gold band isn’t flashy, the way it pairs with her ring makes it feel modern. Since the diamond on her engagement ring has a low-profile setting, it makes it difficult for another band to sit flush beneath the stone. So rather than tucking underneath the diamond, the band rests at the edge of the stone and leaves some negative space free on Dynevor’s finger. Paired with the engagement ring’s bezel setting—which also offers protection to the diamond—the two rings together lend the stone a floating effect.

Dynevor isn’t the only famous bride who has opted for a simpler gold wedding band as of late. Zendaya and her new husband Tom Holland have each stepped out wearing the minimal ring style since their nuptials, and Anne Hathaway also wears one underneath her large emerald-cut diamond engagement ring. As thicker bands and unique settings have become trendier for engagement rings this past year, we’ve also seen many couples choosing to stick with gold bands to balance out these styles.

The style is a classic for a reason. First, the timeless band remains true to the original symbolism of a wedding ring, whose circular shape represents eternity, unbroken commitment, and mutual fidelity. It’s also an excellent choice for those who lean towards practicality. A simple gold band requires very little maintenance, doesn’t risk losing any stones from improper care, and is easy to wear at all times without needing to remove it. Many people also choose to have gold bands as a spacer ring, which can be worn alongside a more elaborate eternity band given for an anniversary gift or push present down the line.

Engagement and wedding ring trends have changed dramatically in recent years. Lab-grown diamonds are now so popular that many to-be-weds have been looking towards bold styles to stand out, from modern, off-center settings to colorful gemstones and antique jewelry pieces. Phoebe Dynevor’s wedding ring might be a sign that amid the search for originality, you shouldn’t ignore the classics.

#6674. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

The two talked modern music, the King’s Trust, and more

The king is officially 78! Charles III, who was born in 1948—just four years before his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, took the throne—celebrated another trip around the sun today. And while the official birthday celebration of the monarch falls in June with the annual Trooping the Colour military parade, the royal family marked his real date of birth with a new portrait of him and Sir. Elton John.

The photo was taken during the taping of a special edition of John’s Apple Music 1 radio show, Rocket Hour, in which the “Tiny Dancer” musician was joined by Charles to mark 50 years of the King’s Trust charity. And in addition to discussing the nonprofit, the two also chatted about modern music, introduced over a dozen hand-selected tracks, and joked about aging.

“We and the Trust are definitely still standing,” the king teased, highlighting the Grammy-winning singer’s “I’m Still Standing” as one of his favorite songs. The musician, from his seat at the table, replied, “I’m still sitting now, though.”

At one point, the monarch gave a particular shoutout to Raye, who he said he “had the pleasure of being introduced to” during a “very memorable performance” at Apple.

A key focus of the Rocket Hour podcast has been to champion emerging artists—a mission that resonates with the King’s Trust’s focus on supporting the next generation. Formerly known as the Prince’s Trust, the organization was founded in 1976 to help young people facing unemployment, homelessness, academic troubles, and more. John has celebrated the charity’s milestones before, even performing at Wembley Arena for the 10th anniversary (1986). In 2001, he joined the royal family for a 25th anniversary dinner at St. James’s Palace in London.

“We are so richly blessed with the talents of our musicians, singers, and performers, particularly yourself, if I may say so,” the king continued, turning to his host. “You’ve become such a national treasure.”

#6671. I Ate Dinner At 6 p.m. For 30 Days—Here’s How My Body Changed

I have always been someone who eats dinner late. Not intentionally, of course, but between deadlines, meetings, and evening errands, food takes a back seat. The result is a familiar one: I end most days uncomfortably bloated and rarely wake up feeling much lighter.

Tired of feeling this way, I challenged myself to something subtle, for the sake of experimenting: to dinner at 6 p.m. for 30 days, without changing what I ate or restricting calories. Would I wake up less bloated? Would I be ravenous before bed? Would my sleep, digestion, or cravings shift? Before starting, I asked two experts whether the clock matters at all.

Laayla Moon, wellness expert and co-founder of Human Upgrade Fest, is not only encouraging about eating dinner early—she’s practically evangelical. “Eating earlier can make a difference for some people, but it’s not necessarily about the magic of 6 p.m.,” she says. The logic is circadian: our digestive system follows a natural rhythm, much like our sleep cycle, and gut activity slows down at night. A heavy meal close to bedtime can leave you feeling full, but also more uncomfortable and prone to acid reflux; on the other hand, a longer gap between dinner and sleep tends to mean a lighter morning. Moon is candid that evidence for a 6 p.m. dinner (or, simply an earlier dinner time) is still limited. “I believe the real takeaway is to eat in harmony with your body’s rhythm rather than follow a rigid clock,” she says.

Rutu Dhodapkar, a clinical dietitian, agrees. “Evening meal timing should be early for getting digestive comfort, as there should be some time for digestion before sleeping,” she explains. In other words, give your body a head start before you lie down. Her recommended cut-off for busy schedules is more forgiving than mine: “For better results in a busy schedule, it’s advised to have meals early—by 8 p.m. or at minimum, two hours before you go to sleep.”

Both experts were quick to add that timing is only one piece of the puzzle. You could dine at 6 p.m. and still wake up bloated if the meal is enormous, rushed, or washed down with something fizzy. As Moon puts it, “how we eat and what we eat can matter just as much as when we eat—and sometimes, more.”

The “how” piece of this equation starts in the mouth. “Eating slowly and chewing as much as possible also helps for better digestion as enzymes get activated,” says Dhodapkar, while eating quickly, swallowing air and reaching for carbonated drinks are classic routes to gas. The “what,” on the other hand, is very personal: legumes and cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and cauliflower can bother people with sensitive guts, and dairy can be a culprit for those who are lactose intolerant. Moon adds a less obvious factor. “I also think we underestimate the gut-brain connection,” she says, which is a polite way of saying that stress and eating on the go doesn’t help.

Dhodapkar’s advice for anyone attempting a trial like mine was refreshingly low-tech: keep a daily diary. She suggests scoring symptoms from one to ten, noting morning bloating, whether an evening walk eases it, bowel movements, hunger, cravings, and sleep quality, alongside stress, hydration, and your menstrual cycle. This will prevent a good week from being mistaken for a breakthrough.

Initially, this experiment came with intense regret. Hunger, mood swings, and a burning rage of irritability took over my late evenings. I even tried going to bed earlier during the first week to avoid hearing the rumbling noises from my stomach.

But by week two, eating dinner early had slowly, if not entirely, become easier. I no longer felt hungry at night, my late-night bloating had reduced and mornings felt much lighter. An unexpected result of this experiment was my renewed ability to distinguish hunger from boredom.

I ended up eating whatever I craved but noticed that I was less inclined to reach for an additional serving. I had developed a newfound appreciation for early dinners and could finally understand why wellness experts and celebrities alike choose to eat early.

Eating early, it turns out, can help digestion, but it is not a magic fix. Moon is clear that “eating earlier is one useful habit, but it isn’t a standalone solution”. The best routine is one that suits your body, schedule and triggers, which means paying attention to portion size, pace and what actually sits well with you.

One caveat: if bloating is persistent or worsening, comes with severe abdominal pain, blood in the stoo,l or unexplained weight loss, no dinner timetable will fix it. See a doctor. The aim, as Moon says, is not to suppress the symptom but to understand what is causing it.

#6670. I Own 400 Sneakers. You Should Only Own 21

I own far too many sneakers. There are everyday beaters, rare samples, and plenty in between, accumulated over more than a decade of collecting. That’s a lot of shoes by any reasonable measure. Around 400 at my last count. A few of my favorites took some work to get. I entered a stupid number of raffles for the JJJJound x New Balance 990v3, lined up overnight for the Sacai x Nike VaporWaffle, and caved and paid resale for the Gucci x Adidas Gazelle.

With that many pairs, you start thinking about what actually earns its space. A shoe can be interesting to collect and difficult to wear. Another can seem almost too obvious to buy, then turn out to be the thing that works with most of your clothes. If I could wipe the slate clean, I’d pay much more attention to that second category. I’d still want some fun stuff, obviously. I’m rebuilding a sneaker collection, not writing a packing list.

So, where would I start? With these 21 pairs from Foot Locker’s selection. There are basketball shoes I’d want for their shape and history, runners I’d buy for everyday wear, and a few low-profile pairs to switch things up. Some are famous enough that they barely need an introduction. But knowing a shoe’s name and knowing why you’d want it in your collection are different things. Here’s why these would make it back into mine.

Yes, four of my first five picks are Nike or Jordan – and that’s deliberate. If I were rebuilding my collection, they’d still get a big chunk of my budget. The Air Jordan 1, Air Force 1, and Dunk are a pretty good explanation for why. If you’re starting with jeans and a tee, I’d look here first. A high-top gives you a little more shoe around the ankle. A low-top is easier with shorts, and white Forces can do a lot of the work when you’re getting dressed in a hurry.

I’d start right here, before getting distracted by anything limited to 200 pairs. Peter Moore’s 1985 design gets the shape so right: the height of the collar, the panels around the toe, the way contrasting colors divide up the upper. The High OG also gives you the Nike Air tongue branding. I want a pair that looks good with straightforward jeans and a tee, and the Air Jordan 1 has been perfecting that combo for decades.

A fresh white Air Force 1 would be an early purchase for the deeply boring reason that I’d wear it constantly. Bruce Kilgore’s 1982 basketball silhouette has enough weight to sit properly under loose jeans, and that beefy sole gives the whole fit a little more presence. White-on-white also makes the leather panels and perforations easier to appreciate. It’s the pair I’d reach for when I like everything else I’m wearing and don’t need to complicate things.

Once you’ve looked at enough Dunks, you notice how much the colorblocking changes the sneaker. Its college basketball background gave those panels a specific purpose: carrying team colors. The ‘Sanded Purple’ makes good use of that layout. I’d want a Dunk Low because the shape is uncomplicated enough to wear regularly, while the colors give an outfit a clear starting point. Pick up one of those shades elsewhere, or leave the rest nice and neutral.

The Superstar arrived as a basketball shoe in 1970; Run-D.M.C.’s “My Adidas” helped give it a very different audience in 1986. That history is good to know, but the Shelltoe is what would get my money. It gives the front of the shoe a distinctive shape, and the Superstar II’s extra padding makes the whole thing feel chunkier than the OG. I’d put these under straight jeans, with enough of the toe showing to appreciate it.

The High would come first, of course, but I’d still make room for an Air Jordan 1 Low OG. Removing the tall collar changes how the panels sit with your pants, giving you more space around the ankle and a less bulky-looking sneaker. I’d buy it for days when I want that familiar Jordan colorblocking with shorts or slightly shorter pants. There’s enough difference to justify the second box.

For a day with a lot of walking, I’d start with the 990v6 or the Zoom Vomero 5. There are plenty of ways to get that mesh running-shoe look, and the XT-6 is the one I’d pick if I wanted a trail sole with more grip.

Yes, there would absolutely be gray New Balances in the rebuild. The 990 family started in 1982, but the sixth-gen adds FuelCell cushioning and lets the suede overlays flow across the mesh without the usual midfoot saddle. You can see the difference, and there’s a practical benefit underfoot, too. This is the pair I’d buy for days with a lot of walking: comfy enough to justify the purchase, good-looking enough that comfort isn’t the only justification.

The OG 2008 Gel-Kayano 14 was the first in the series designed by someone other than Toshikazu Kayano – useful information for your next deeply specific sneaker convo. More relevant here is how well the layered mesh and synthetic overlays work together. The ‘Graphite Grey’ has enough contrast to show off the construction, with Gel cushioning right underneath.

The 1906R is for when I want all the little technical details. Open mesh, curvy overlays, and segmented cushioning around the heel give you plenty to check out, especially in white, silver, and black. It shares the same sole tech with the 2002R and 860v2, but the upper just looks more put-together.

The Zoom Vomero 5 launched back in 2011, but it didn’t gain its cult following until about a decade later. There’s a lot to enjoy up top: open mesh, overlapping panels, and plastic caging that becomes particularly obvious in ‘Metallic Silver’. Zoom Air cushioning gives it a practical role in the collection, too. I’d buy this as a regular-wear pair for long days, with enough detail to make jeans and a plain sweater look put together.

First released in 2010, the Omni 9 has all the mesh and supporting structure you’d expect from a running shoe of that era. This white and pink version lets you see how the layers fit together, with ProGrid cushioning underneath. I’d want it because a collection can become very repetitive once you find a couple of brands you like. The Omni gives me another interpretation of the technical runner, with enough character to earn its place alongside the Nikes and Asics.

The P-6000 looks like a straight archive reissue, but it actually combines elements from the Pegasus 25 and Pegasus 2006. I’d buy the white and silver combo and wear the hell out of them – every pair doesn’t need to be an occasion.

The XT-6 started life in 2013 as a serious trail running shoe, and you can still see that purpose in the reinforced upper, Quicklace system, and lugged outsole. My plans would probably involve considerably less altitude. I’d buy it because the close-fitting upper and outdoor construction bring something different to the collection, particularly with cargo pants or wider-leg pants. The ‘Black Coffee’ also makes it easy to wear with denim, olive, and navy. No hiking itinerary required.

If your jeans taper or you like a shorter hem, try something that sits closer to the foot. The Samba is an easy place to start in black leather. I’d go for the green Spezial if I wanted a little color without having to think too hard about the rest of the fit.

Collecting can make you weird about buying something that everybody else owns – I’d try to avoid that with the Samba. Its roots go back to soccer shoes for icy fields in 1950, but the slim shape is what earns it a place here. After a few chunky basketball shoes, you need something that sits closer to the foot. ‘Core Black’ leather, white stripes, and a suede T-toe give you plenty to work with, particularly under a straighter pair of pants.

Yes, there’s already a Samba here. The Handball Spezial earns its own place with its rounded toe, suede upper, and gum sole, which give it a softer appearance than the leather-heavy pairs. First made for handball players in 1979, it’s also a good way to bring some color into the rebuild. The green and white do enough on their own. I’d wear these with blue jeans and let the suede take care of the rest.

The Gazelle dates back to 1966, making this year its 60th birthday. I’d buy it for the suede upper and the straightforward proportions, which give it a slightly different feel from the other Adidas silhouettes here. In black and white, it’s easy to wear with faded denim or dark pants. Some days, a familiar shape in simple colors is exactly what you want.

Puma’s Suede history runs back to 1968, so I’d want some of that history in the collection, as well as the shoe’s simple construction. The soft upper and sweeping Formstrip give you texture and shape without a bunch of extra panels. It would be a useful change after several technical runners, especially with denim or cotton pants that already have plenty of texture themselves.

Wide jeans and heavier layers can take a bigger shoe. I’d look at the Air Max 95 for the layered upper, the Gel-NYC if I wanted something a little quieter, or the 9060 if I wanted the sole to do most of the talking.

Sergio Lozano was inspired by human anatomy for the Air Max 95, translating ribs, muscle fibers, and a spine into a running shoe. A pretty weird design concept that produced a very good sneaker. Those layered side panels are the reason I’d buy it again: they give the shoe depth even in this low-key black, white, and gray combination. It has enough bulk for wider pants, and enough going on that the rest of the fit can stay simple.

The Gel-NYC looks pretty old school, but Asics actually assembled it from several archive references. There’s Gel-Nimbus 3 and Gel-MC Plus V in the upper, with Gel-Cumulus 16 tooling underneath. The result has a fuller shape than the Kayano, with more emphasis on those broad suede panels. That’s why I’d make room for both. This ‘Cream’ and ‘Oyster Grey’ version works particularly well beneath wider pants, where a very slim shoe can disappear under the hem.

A collection of completely sensible sneakers would feel like an opportunity missed. The 9060 takes details from New Balance’s 99X family and blows them up: the 990’s sway bars spread across the upper, while the sole gets a sculpted, pod-like shape. I’d pick this brown version to balance out bigger pants and heavier layers. It gives those clothes a chunky enough shoe to sit over.

These are the two I’d happily get dirty. Go for the Chucks if you like a high-top with cuffed jeans, or the Old Skools if you want something low that’s just as easy to wear with shorts.

Black canvas Chucks would be back on the shelf pretty quickly, too. Their basketball DNA stretches all the way back to 1917, but it’s the narrow shape I’d want in this collection. It gives jeans a completely different finish from an AF1 or a 990, especially with a little ankle showing. These are also shoes I’d be happy to wear until the canvas softened and the rubber picked up some marks.

To finish off my new collection, I’d grab a pair of Old Skools. Launched in 1977 as the Style 36, it introduced the Jazz Stripe along the way. The canvas-and-suede upper, white stripe, and waffle sole are still enough to make it worth owning. It looks good with jeans, works with shorts, and improves once the upper loosens up. After all the comparing and researching and rebuilding, I’d want at least one pair I could put on and forget about.

#6669. Steven Spielberg Believes Empathy Is Our ‘Only Real Superpower’

The veteran filmmaker was honored at the 18th annual MoMA Film Benefit with Chanel.

As rain poured down on Manhattan Thursday night, so did the tributes to Steven Spielberg. The veteran director was honored at this year’s MoMA Film Benefit, presented by Chanel, with homages from fellow icons of cinema and collaborators including Martin Scorsese, Tom Cruise, Emily Blunt, and Ariana DeBose. To top off the night, Spielberg (and the crowd) was treated to a surprise acoustic performance by Bruce Springsteen.

Honoring Spielberg’s contributions to film feels like a no-brainer, given the dozens of masterpieces he has delivered in his decades-long career, spanning Jaws, E.T., the Indiana Jones franchise, Schindler’s List, Jurassic Park, Saving Private Ryan, and many more, all the way up to Disclosure Day, which was just released this summer. Reflecting on his latest, Spielberg said in his speech, “It’s less about aliens and more about empathy. Empathy is the only real superpower that humanity possesses. It’s the only form of magic, I think, that exists in the world.”

And while he accepted the honor solo, the director said he shares the recognition with the hundreds of people in his casts and crews, including those who work at craft services. He also took a moment to thank his wife.

“When you honor me, you are also honoring my wife, Kate Capshaw, because the stuff I put in each of my films is from the stuff of life, real life, that Kate and I have created with family, friends, and conversation, and being aware that there’s more to living than just what we do for a living,” he said. “The confidence she’s given me every day for the past 43 years, I would not be the same person, or the same filmmaker, without her central to my very human existence.”

The program included opening remarks from Cruise, who starred in Minority Report and War of the Worlds, followed by a speech from Scorsese, who reflected on his decades of friendship with Spielberg. “Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972—how did we get to be in our eighties? What happened?” he joked. DeBose, who starred in Spielberg’s West Side Story remake and won an Oscar, performed “Somewhere” from the legendary musical.

Blunt, who starred in Disclosure Day, revealed that the back of Spielberg’s director’s chair is labeled with “Dad.” “‘Dad’ still has this childlike enthusiasm, this spontaneity,” she said. And when he’s “happy with a take, you’ll see him, he’ll just come running out of the tent with his fists in the air, and he’s cheering, and it’s like the best damn moment of your career,” she added. Spielberg later returned the praise, saying Blunt “could play any role—including James Bond.”

Steve Martin and Martin Short alternated zippy one-liners while introducing the guest of honor (they even joked about how many awards they shared between the three of them). And Stephen Colbert helped introduce the grand finale, Bruce Springsteen, who sang “Dancing in the Dark” on his guitar. Before jumping into song, The Boss took a moment to say a few words about Spielberg too, recalling the summer when Jaws first came out when he was living on the Jersey Shore. There used to be a tradition called night swimming, where people would swim in the ocean nude, often with someone they were interested in. But ever since Jaws, “Steven Spielberg fucked that up. He fucked it up good,” Springsteen said, to a room of laughter.

Other attendees included Drew Barrymore, Cate Blanchett, Robert De Niro, Jeff Goldblum, Riley Keough, John Krasinski, Donna Langley, Spike Lee, Lorne Michaels, Michelle Pfeiffer, Zoe Saldaña, Francesca Scorsese, Christopher Walken, and Michelle Williams. Jennifer Lawrence and Cooke Maroney made a low-key appearance.

#6668. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6666. The Best New Restaurants in New York City to Visit Now

For some New Yorkers, keeping up with the city’s ever-changing restaurant scene is something of a sport. Indeed, there seems to be a hot new place every week, and sometimes the cadence of openings—as well as rising chefs, new concepts, and freshly renovated rooms—can make your head spin. Of course, there are always the old haunts, the standbys—but isn’t it fun to have some new players on the scene?

There are plenty of fresh restaurants this fall, so if you’re looking for the best and buzziest new restaurants to add to your list, Vogue has you covered. For this list, we focused on places that opened in the past three months. There’s the trio of Bangkok women bringing heartwarming Thai food to a homey West Village space, an Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery from an award-winning chef, a beloved South Indian pop-up turned brick-and-mortar gem, and more.

Below, read our picks for the best new restaurants in New York City.

Tucked along the westernmost stretch of Christopher Street, this new Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie is making everyone’s mornings a bit cheerier with its sorghum banana bread and beef patty croissants. Calabash opened its doors in early October and is Chef Camari Mick’s first solo restaurant following her role as executive pastry chef of the Musket Room and Raf’s. (She opened alongside chef de cuisine Tajeh Porter.) Daytime service is great for grabbing laminated pastries and breakfast sandwiches from the case, but if you have time to sit down, the fluffy cornbread pancakes drizzled with salted maple sabayon just might ruin all future pancakes for you.

And if you’re really ready to commit (trust me, you are), they’re also offering a five-course prix fixe served Friday and Saturday evenings, with one seating at 6:30 p.m. Dishes like Hoppin’ John Dolma wrapped in collard greens, and red snapper with sweet corn and étouffée-style gravy explore the connections between the diaspora and classical techniques, and are paired with house-fermented mocktails. The restaurant is named for the vessel that has traveled across the African diaspora throughout history, and Chef Mick’s menu highlights traditions found across West Africa, the Caribbean, and America’s Eastern seaboard. As if all of that wasn't worth firing up your OpenTable, I’ve yet to mention the interiors. The 30-seat, 1,300-square-foot space was designed by D.C.-based Drummond Projects (very cozy, very refined), and they also partnered with gallerist Cierra Britton on an exhibition of paintings by BIPOC women artists. —Nicole Kliest, contributing writer

Turn the corner onto East Broadway, past the bustling crowds of Bar Oliver, and you’ll find Cavalier, a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant and wine bar from Chef Mason Lindahl, Tate Jackson, and Yasmin Kaytmaz (who also owns The River). They’ve got pink tables, black leather booths, low lighting, and a private dining room in the back with a dreamlike mural by Georgia Gardner Gray.

The vibe at Cavalier is friendly and earnest, a welcome contrast to the sometimes aloof, cooler-than-thou energy of some of the other nearby see-and-be-seen spots. But the real star here is Chef Lindahl’s food, which feels fancy and comforting all at once. You’ll want to get at least one order of the baked lavash bread, which is served with tomato butter and eggplant, and is so warm and soft you could curl up and take a nap in it.

I also loved the chicken liver mousse, the tender and flavorful duck, and the chocolate mousse for dessert. Double mousse, yes: If it seems decadent, it is, but somehow you leave feeling lighter. They also have what my wine friends call a “serious” wine list, with extensive bottle offerings and fun by-the-glass options, including a red blend from Château Musar, the cult-favorite Lebanese producer. —Anna Grace Lee, lifestyle writer

The vibes might be pleasantly low-key at this new Mexican seafood spot in the West Village, but the food and wine are worth planning an entire evening around. El Camarón Peludo opened this past September on Cornelia Street (next door to the now shuttered Pearl Oyster Bar) and was conceived by the team behind Taqueria Ramirez and Carnitas Ramírez, Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar, as well as Mexico City-born chef Carlos Barrera. The restaurant is walk-in only, and feels like the love child of a Spanish tapas bar and a quintessential Mexican kitchen.

By their own admission, the menu is an unapologetic celebration of shrimp (all hail the cute crustacean!). Order them raw, chilled, grilled, boiled, or otherwise, and your taste buds are in for a ride. In fact, there’s even a shrimp-shaped lantern hanging above the raw bar, if you appreciate commitment to a theme. Complement all that freshness with their salsa, like the one made from four different chiles, and a wine selection that will knock your socks off. —N.K.

Straker’s is an exercise in controlled chaos. The first New York outpost from Thomas Straker, the TikTok-famous British chef known for his namesake Notting Hill restaurant and “bad boy” reputation, Straker’s is a place where the room is loud, the bouncer wears leather, and the food is excellent.

When I went on a Tuesday a few weeks after opening, the room seemed full of vaguely businessy men and models, everyone’s faces blurring in candlelight, the glow interrupted by the flash of phones eating first. Is this the place to come for a long overdue catch-up with a friend, or a first date? No. I want to come here with three friends and sit in the corner sipping martinis while the loud, untz-untz music bass-shakes the banquettes and drowns out our gossip.

I could easily eat two of the wood-fired mussel flatbread, which is like pizza crust dipped in buttery mussel sauce. The duck was tender, the potatoes perfectly crispy. Dessert is also important. The rainbow array of ice creams is sure to spark debate (we went with the burnt honey, which was nice and not too sweet), but no matter what you do, get the chocolate tart. Don’t skip the cucumber salad either, which offered a pleasingly fresh crunch to balance out the indulgence—though indulgence is the name of the game here. That is, of course, if you can get a reservation. —A.G.L.

Adding to the city’s dynamic supper club scene, chef Lana Lagomarsini opened Creola on the Upper East Side this past September, following her time as chef de cuisine at Francis Mallmann’s Garzón in Uruguay, as well as cooking stints at Gramercy Tavern, Daniel, and Momofuku Ko. The opening menu kicked off with flavors like elk with blackberry jerk and plantain, and an oxtail pâté en croûte (evoking a Jamaican beef patty). The wines are sourced from low-intervention producers from France and Spain, and can either be paired with each course or purchased by the glass or bottle. (Top points for the fact that every bottle is priced under $100!) Fortify your appetite for dessert, which at the moment is a sassafras flan crowned with a poached cherry and bay leaf oil.

The restaurant’s name is a sentimental homage to Lagomarsini’s grandmother, Creola, who lived on the Upper West Side and crossed Central Park every afternoon to pick her up from school, located just five blocks from where the restaurant now stands. There’s even a framed photo of her grandmother that hangs in the dining room, which makes the experience feel all the more intimate and homey. Speaking of the interiors, the design was impressively handled by Lagomarsini herself, who sourced antique furniture and hemmed the curtains by hand. Creola has 12 seats and is open Wednesday through Saturday beginning at 5 p.m. with two seatings a night. —N.K.

When I heard that the Portuguese chef Nuno Sousa—of Leitão in the West Village, where I’ve enjoyed tapas and not-too-sweet margaritas—was opening a new restaurant nearby on West 10th Street, I was curious to try it. Galo, which is in a historic 1860s carriage house, is a warm space decorated with ceramic art where you can have suckling pig, octopus that slices as smooth as butter, and tender picanha. They have an extensive Portuguese wine list, but I loved the Só mais uma cocktail (a refreshing mojito-like mix of gin, matcha, mint, lime, and Portuguese herbal liqueur), and the potato pavé, which was crispy and crunchy like thin slices of potato paper. —A.G.L.

Hommali is the debut restaurant from a team of three Thai women—chef Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak “Picha” Srigungvarl—all Bangkok natives who became friends while working in the New York City restaurant scene. They’ve put a lot of hometown heart into Hommali, which takes its name from hom mali, which is Thai for “fragrant jasmine rice.”

You can feel the camaraderie in the air of the cozy West Village space. Paintings from Bangkok’s Chatuchak Weekend Market line the walls of the den-like downstairs dining room, and dishes like tom yum seafood cocktail are served in a beautiful shell. I loved the Panang curry beef cheek and the five-spice duck with duck fat rice, plus the passionfruit cocktail with a bubble-bath-like topping, and delicious toasted rice ice cream with coconut for dessert. —A.G.L.

Over the past few years, Top Chef alum Rasika Venkatesa has built up a devoted following with her Mythily pop-ups. Now, Chef Venkatesa’s progressive South Indian restaurant has found a brick-and-mortar home in Williamsburg. Named in honor of Venkatesa’s grandmother, the restaurant draws on her childhood in Chennai, techniques she learned while traveling across Tamil Nadu, and her fine-dining training at The French Laundry and Mourad.

When I went for dinner not long after its opening in late September, every table was full. People craned their necks to look at the vibrant, artful dishes landing on each table. I got my spoon out to scoop up all the delicious, creamy sauce of the Lamb Sukka Dumplings, which is a must-order, along with the Benne Dosa, the chicken, and the confit potato roast with sambar béarnaise, plus the “filter coffee soft-serve.” —A.G.L.

Some of my most memorable meals have been in Brazil (first time ant consumption, for example), and while I don’t have immediate travel plans to return to the South American culinary capital, thankfully, I have Iara. Chef Vitor Mendes’s new restaurant in the Lower East Side takes inspiration from the Amazon Rainforest and is named for the region’s water goddess. The 60-seat, open-kitchen concept was designed by New York-based practice Studio WDM and channels the Amazon’s soil for its painterly color palette (swirls of chocolate brown, burnt oranges, and terracotta dance across the walls and tables).

Menu-wise, it’s basically a who’s who of Amazonian heavyweight flavors: tapioca crisps gilded with smoked trout mousse and biquinho pepper, cheese bread with smoked eggplant dip, Brazilian red snapper stew with red palm dendê oil, tucupi, and coconut milk. If you’re looking to impress your dining mate, go for the charcoal-grilled tambaqui, a large Amazonian river fish that the team brushes with a spice blend and serves alongside stewed butter beans, tapioca fries, and açaí ketchup. —N.K.

These days, the word “sexy” is thrown around a lot when describing a restaurant, but 148 Noble actually is sexy. The French and New Orleans-inspired bistro, on a quiet residential street in Greenpoint, is candlelit and cozy. It’s small, but not too small. The service is attentive, with a slightly conspiratorial air that makes you feel like you’re all in on the same secret. A misstep is corrected by a heavier-than-usual wine pour. Yes, the portions might be a bit small, but every bite is flavorful. The chef, Gabriel Borges, is from New Orleans and used to work at Chez Ma Tante down the street. Bring your date and get the pommes paillasson (a Jenga tower of fancy French fries, basically), the duck with honeynut squash and pickled ají dulce, and the rich chocolate tarte with crème fraîche. —A.G.L.

Why have a normal-portioned meal when an all-you-can-eat buffet is an option? It’s a fair question to ask yourself prior to arriving at Good Time Country Buffet, which translates a cherished Southern dining tradition to the East Village. This is the third restaurant from Good Time Hospitality, the same team behind Kisa and C as in Charlie. If you’ve been to either of the aforementioned hotspots, you’re already aware the team was born in Korea and raised in Atlanta, with both of these distinct culinary identities cleverly finding their way onto the menus.

For this concept, they turned to the classic buffets they grew up going to, and programmed the menu to be a fixed-price, self-serve extravaganza. Fried chicken, collard greens, cornbread, mac and cheese, ice cream sundaes—the sky’s the limit, friends. And as far as inspiration goes, they didn’t stop at the menus. The interiors were designed by Two Point Zero and echo classic country buffets with wood paneling, patterned wallpapers, and—rather thoughtfully—carpeted floors, which traditionally have been used to ensure seniors don’t slip and fall while getting their buffet on. (Seniors coming to Good Time Country Buffet also receive a discounted price.) This opening especially strikes a chord with co-owner David Yun, who, as a kid, joined produce delivery routes to Georgia country buffets with his father, who still works in the same role. As part of the restaurant’s research and development process, Yun rejoined his father on those routes. —N.K.

Humm, Daniel Humm’s first namesake restaurant, is about as buzzy as it gets. The cavernous 7,731-square-foot space—which was home to EN Japanese Brasserie for 20 years—has been transformed by Humm and interior designer Pierre Yovanovitch, along with artists Francesco Clemente and Rashid Johnson. The room glows with light from taper candles encased in glass on each table. A sunset tile mural frames the 16-foot wood-fired hearth oven, and it all feels a little like being in another world for the night. Everyone gets the caviar bagel, which is good (it’s a miniature bagel with caviar, after all), but my favorite dishes were the tomato focaccia and the milk and honey soft-serve sundae. —A.G.L.

In a sea of nostalgic-themed restaurants, Booth’s Extra Fine should go to the top of your must-try list. It’s not a club masquerading as a steakhouse; it’s the real deal. Chef Nick Pfannerstill, who worked at the now-closed Michelin-starred restaurant Dovetail and is co-owner of the cocktail bar Nobody Told Me, is serving smoky steaks that cast a pleasant aroma over the room, cold and balanced martinis, a butter roll that glistens, Caesar salad with garlic bread-like croutons, shrimp voodoo. Everything I had was delicious, and it was fun to try various sauces on offer, including salsa verde and aged brandy peppercorn. For dessert, get the bourbon chocolate cake, which may fulfill my years-long search for a chocolate cake as decadent as the one in Matilda. —A.G.L.

#6665. ELLE Escapes: Río Grande

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Puerto Rico has long been one of my favorite island destinations for a little rest and relaxation. Time and again, I find myself drawn back to the charming towns dotted along its northern and northeastern coasts. This month, my travels brought me to Río Grande, a tranquil, picturesque municipality affectionately known as La Ciudad de El Yunque (The City of El Yunque).

Just a 30-minute drive from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, Río Grande offers a calmer setting than the bustling streets of San Juan, while still keeping the capital city’s attractions within easy reach. Beloved for its lush landscapes, breathtaking scenery, and abundant flora and fauna, the area is also home to a significant portion of El Yunque National Forest, which, fun fact, is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System.

Whether you prefer lounging poolside with a piña colada, venturing into the rainforest for a scenic hike, or heading west to meander through the vibrant streets of Old San Juan, I’ve found that Río Grande makes for an idyllic home base to experience the best of what the island has to offer.

Ahead, discover my recommendations for where to stay, what to eat, and what to explore in this enchanting corner of Puerto Rico.

Taking a nature walk or scenic hike through El Yunque National Forest is a must when visiting Río Grande. Whether you book a guided tour or venture out on your own with a rental car, there are trails suited to every experience level. Along the way, you’ll be stunned by the sheer variety of plants and wildlife you encounter. On my trip, I finally put a face to the symphony of chirps I’d been hearing throughout my stay: the Puerto Rican spindalis, a small, yellow-bellied bird native to the island.

The forest is also home to a seemingly endless variety of tropical trees, mushrooms, orchids, and ferns. Climb the spiral staircase of the Yokahú Observation Tower for panoramic views of the lush green canopy and surrounding mountain peaks, and be sure to pack water shoes if you fancy a refreshing dip in one of the forest’s rivers or natural waterfall pools.

Whether you’re an avid golfer or just getting into the sport, Río Grande has several world-class courses worth exploring. Among them is Bahía Beach Golf Club, an 18-hole, par-72 course designed by renowned golf course architect Robert Trent Jones Jr. in 2008. Stretching 6,890 yards through lush tropical landscapes, the course features 15 holes bordering water, with beautiful rainforest views along the way. You’ll wind around scenic lakes before reaching the Atlantic coastline for the final few holes, making for an unforgettable morning or afternoon on the green.

Set sail from the nearby town of Fajardo for a morning, afternoon, or all-day affair spent exploring nearby islands with seemingly untouched beaches. Popular destinations include Culebra and Icacos Island, where you can lounge on the boat, soak up the sun, swim in crystal-clear waters, or snorkel among vibrant coral reefs teeming with colorful fish.

Perla, located at Four Seasons, opened this November under the direction of executive chef Victor Rosado and became one of my favorite dining spots during my visit. Taking its name from the Spanish word for “pearl,” the elegant restaurant offers a tempting selection of small bites, from pillowy Parker House rolls served with smoked butter to spicy salmon mousse, alongside standout seafood dishes like hamachi and Chilean sea bass.

The thoughtfully designed interior boasts natural wood accents and bold contemporary artwork, with sweeping ocean views to admire between courses. As for what to order, don’t miss the oyster brûlée with yuzu kosho hollandaise and crispy Ibérico ham, the prime New York strip steak served with Hasselback potatoes, or the tender octopus accompanied by creamy potato causa.

For lunch, head to Don Pepe, a longtime local favorite where the atmosphere is casual and the focus is on authentic Puerto Rican cooking made with quality ingredients and bold flavors. The menu spans traditional favorites like beef piononos and mofongo served with your choice of protein and sauce, alongside heartier, mouthwatering dishes like succulent grilled pork loin, the restaurant’s signature burger, and lobster risotto. The extensive cocktail menu also offers a tempting selection of tropical concoctions made with locally produced Don Q rum.

Another recent addition to the dining options at the Four Seasons Resort is Ocean Terrace, a picturesque open-air restaurant set along the shoreline. Open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, the restaurant has a varied menu with something to satisfy every craving.

Mornings begin with a generous breakfast buffet, and if you have a sweet tooth like me, the coquito French toast on the à la carte menu is a must-try. For lunch, you’ll find everything from truffle honey stracciatella served with ciabatta to salads, pizzas, and sandwiches. Come dinnertime, I’d recommend exploring the selection of freshly made pastas, especially the creamy carbonara with pancetta—a dish I’m still dreaming about.

When you’re in the mood for a glamorous, atmospheric lounge to sip cocktails, head to Palm Court. The sleek, modern interior features plush seating that invites you to settle in and unwind, while a grand, square-shaped white marble bar serves as the room’s centerpiece. Beyond the elegant interior, an outdoor terrace offers additional seating for those who prefer to dine or enjoy a drink in the warm ocean breeze.

Located at the Bahía Beach Club, Sugar Beach Bar is a laid-back, open-air spot serving flavorful cocktails and delicious shareable bites. Sip on a tasty tropical cocktail made with local rum or tequila while soaking up stunning views of the ocean waves and Sugar Beach Pool.

Situated right by the Bahía Beach driving range, El Cocoteros Grill is a casual spot to unwind with a local beer. Open for breakfast and lunch, the restaurant offers a relaxed atmosphere, modern furnishings, and scenic rainforest views. And if you’re out on the golf course, you can even have drinks delivered straight to your golf cart.

You can always count on a five-star stay at a Four Seasons, and the recently opened Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, nestled within the picturesque Bahía Beach community, is no exception. Set across 483 acres of spectacular tropical landscape, the resort boasts 104 guest rooms, 35 luxurious suites, and an impressive collection of private residences. The property has rightfully earned a coveted Michelin Key in recognition of its exceptional grounds, hospitality, and dining.

The accommodations are everything you’d expect from the hotel company, with luxe, modern furnishings, 24-hour in-room dining, and an attentive concierge team that can arrange everything from dinner reservations to rainforest excursions. The location also doubles as a private nature reserve, with conservation efforts that include rain gardens and sea turtle nesting protection. Guests can explore the surrounding wildlife and tropical flora through guided nature experiences, all without leaving the vicinity. And if you find yourself wishing you could stay a little longer, the dreamy private residences offer a more permanent escape to paradise.

As for how to spend your days, take your pick among lounging along the resort’s two miles of pristine beachfront, cooling off in one of the two swimming pools, or heading out to explore the island.

A golf lover’s dream, Bahía Beach Resort & Golf Club offers a more residential take on the traditional resort experience. Visitors can enjoy a private getaway in one of the community’s luxurious villas and residences, many of which are available for short-term rentals. Among them is Paradise View Villa, an incredible two-bedroom, three-bathroom property that comes with a six-passenger golf cart for getting around the grounds. Guests also have access to an array of resort amenities, including the golf club, tennis facilities, a fitness center, and the Lakehouse, where a variety of water sports await.

Ideal for families, larger groups, or those planning a special celebration, Wyndham Grand Rio Mar has 400 guest rooms, including 40 spacious suites with refined, colorful furnishings. With so much to see and do on the property, you could easily spend your entire getaway without venturing beyond the resort. Indulge in restorative treatments at El Yunque Spa, spend a lazy afternoon under the sun on the beach, or enjoy a round of golf at the scenic Rio Mar Country Club.

#6664. The Stars Brought the Glamour to the 2026 Baby2Baby Gala Presented by Paul Mitchell

Harper’s Bazaar has exclusive snapshots from the event’s portrait studio

Every year, the Baby2Baby Gala brings together the biggest names in philanthropy, entertainment, and fashion for an evening of fundraising and celebration. And last night, the 15th edition was no exception—with the likes of Demi Moore, Andrew Garfield, Jessica Alba, Barbara Palvin and Dylan Sprouse, Kerry Washington, and Katy Perry showing up in West Hollywood to support the organization’s mission to help kids in need.

From the gala’s inception, Baby2Baby co-CEOS Norah Weinstein and Kelly Sawyer Patricof wanted to create an event that felt “less like a traditional fundraiser.” Year after year, the night has offered its star-studded guests more than just an excuse to get dressed up and a chance to make a difference with their wallets—pairing fundraising efforts with exclusive dining experiences from top chefs and intimate performances from award-winning musicians. (Last night, Carbone flew in from New York City and Cardi B took the stage.)

“We wanted to create an event that would appeal to a younger generation of donors through our approach to food, fashion, and celebrity, while making sure that nobody left the gala without understanding our mission,” Weinstein and Patricof told Harper’s Bazaar. “Fifteen years later, the gala has evolved in ways we never could have imagined, but some themes have stayed exactly the same. Every flower and fork is underwritten by our generous sponsors so that every dollar raised can go directly to Baby2Baby and the children we serve.”

Each year, the funds raised from the gala help get millions of basic essentials—from diapers to formula to clothing—to children who need them. But the organization, with an all-female board of directors, spends all year working towards the Baby2Baby mission. “The gala brings this extraordinary community together for one night, but it’s their commitment throughout the year that makes our work possible,” the CEOs shared.
