#6583. Cream Cheese Mashed Potatoes

Cream cheese doesn't just belong on bagels. In this instance, it's the secret to making mashed potatoes even creamier, richer, and more decadent. The high fat content in the cream cheese melds with the butter and milk to make the potatoes perfectly fluffy and creamy. Serve these at your Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner, or even on a cozy weeknight alongside oven-baked pork chops.

What People Are Saying:“Never cooked mashed potatoes before, and this recipe turned out amazing.” - GreenHat

“Silky smooth and delicious” - BlueProcessor

In a large pot, cover the potatoes with water and season with salt. Bring it to a boil and cook until the potatoes are softened and fork-tender, which should take about 16 to 18 minutes. Drain and return the potatoes to the pot.

Add cream cheese and, using a potato masher, mash potatoes until smooth.

Meanwhile, in a small saucepan over medium heat, cook the milk and butter. Stir until the butter is melted, which should take about 2 minutes. Pour the butter mixture over the potatoes.

Stir until it's combined and creamy. Make sure to season with salt and pepper!

Transfer potatoes to a serving bowl and season with more pepper. Top with chives and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover cream cheese mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6582. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6579. Andrew Garfield’s Hair Is the Mane Attraction

Andrew Garfield’s hair is very long—and oh so glorious. When the 43-year-old actor sat down with GQ for his 2026 Men of the Year interview, he told us he’d grown his current shoulder-length mane for his role as Roy Horn (of Siegfried & Roy tiger-wrangling fame) in the upcoming series Wild Things. Production ultimately put him in a wig, but Garfield kept the length regardless. And thank goodness he did. The actor brought his enviable mane to the red carpet at our annual Men of the Year party at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles on Thursday night, where it held its own among Hollywood’s finest.

The Artificial star arrived in an Edward Sexton suit, accessorized with a Breguet watch. But, as has been the case lately, his hair was the real headliner. The neck-grazing length was in fine form, with a few stray strands tucked neatly behind his ears. And then there was the forehead curl: a particularly on-trend flourish that’s found its place atop some of this year’s best-dressed stars (including Ayo Edebiri).

We first caught a glimpse of Garfield’s longer locks at Wimbledon this summer in London. At the time, his longtime hairstylist, Lucy Halperin, let us in on the secret to the look: a little sea salt spray, styling cream, and a diffuser to bring out his natural curls and waves. The combination enhances the hair’s volume while keeping frizz at bay.

That said, Halperin also credits his good hair to a bit of genetic luck. “Sometimes we just give it a good little wet down, and it kind of just works with him,” she told us at the time.

Whatever transformations Garfield has in store for his next on-screen role, we hope this particular look sticks around. Because if Thursday night was any indication, he’s not quite ready to part with it—and frankly, neither are we.

#6578. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6577. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6576. Turkey Cheese Ball

The turkey may be the main event of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can be a snack, too! Whether you're hosting Thanksgiving for your community or celebrating with family, this fun appetizer is the perfect way to get everyone excited for the big turkey dinner with another smaller turkey! This cheese ball is not only the most eye-catching appetizer you can add to your holiday menu, but it’s surprisingly easy to create.

What People Are Saying:“I made this for Friendsgiving. It was delicious and I got several comments on how great it tasted.” - kellykcox34580

In a food processor, pulse the cream cheese, goat cheese, butter, and garlic powder until the mixture is smooth. Add parsley, chives, and thyme and pulse until well combined. Then season with salt and black pepper.

Transfer the cream cheese mixture to a piece of plastic wrap and gather up the wrap to form a ball. Then transfer the mixture into a large bowl and refrigerate until it’s firm, which should take at least three hours and up to one day.

In a clean food processor, pulse 3/4 cup pecan halves until they are finely chopped.

Roll the cheese ball in nuts and arrange it all on a platter.

Start by cutting a large triangle from a red bell pepper—this will be the face. Next, cut a smaller triangle from a yellow bell pepper for the beak. For the eyes, slice two small rounds from a small carrot. Take a larger carrot and slice it into diagonal ovals to make the feet, then carve little triangles at one end to look like toes. Finally, thinly slice the rest of the carrots into matchsticks for the tail.

Grab some toothpicks and stick the carrot eyes onto the red triangle face. Then, use another toothpick to add the yellow beak to the face—just make sure all the toothpicks point toward the back so you can attach everything to the cheese ball later. Now, press the face onto the front of the cheese ball, and slide the carrot feet into the base.

Insert matchstick carrots, pretzel sticks, and mini pretzels into the back of the ball to create the tail. Using the remaining 1/2 cup pecan halves, create wings by overlapping them along each side of the ball. Serve with crackers alongside!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover cheese ball in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. If possible, remove the pretzels and vegetable decorations before storing, as they can soften over time.

#6575. Read Dodie Kazanjian’s In-Depth 1994 Richard Avedon Profile for Vogue

“Avedon’s Eye,” by Dodie Kazanjian, was originally published in the February 1994 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

Richard Avedon made four trips to Stockholm a few years ago to see Ingmar Bergman’s production of Long Day’s Journey into Night, in Swedish. He saw it seven times. “There’s no movie I could see seven times, but when a great living performance captures me, I could go every night, forever . . . . At the Royal Dramatic Theater in Stockholm, when you go upstairs for coffee during intermission, there’s a place on the ceiling where they have the masks of comedy and tragedy—and they’re both tragedy! Because you’re in Sweden. So it’s the perfect place for me, obviously.”

There’s some irony here but also a valid point. Theater is the guiding metaphor in Richard Avedon’s life, as well as his work. An element of drama gets into everything he does, and the last few months have certainly brought him center stage. The most famous American photographer of our time has been up to his ears in publicity (and controversy) over his recently published book of photographs—which he calls An Autobiography—and over the major retrospective of his work that opens on March 24 at the Whitney Museum. Attention is being paid: 30 pages in Newsweek on the man and his work; appearances on Prime-Time Live, the Today show, and Charlie Rose; a black-tie gala at the New York Public Library for 300 people, thrown by husband-and-wife team Harold Evans, head of Random House (which published An Autobiography), and Tina Brown, The New Yorker’s editor, who a year ago made Avedon the magazine’s first and only staff photographer. At the age of 70, Avedon has shifted his half-century career into overdrive, but somehow he still manages to find time to make dinner arrangements with this reporter for a gourmet meal that he cooks himself.

In a manner of speaking, that is. “You call this cooking?” Dick scoffs, in his unmistakable rasp—New York accented but with other ingredients, mostly untraceable. “I’m an executive cook,” he says. Verlie Fisher, his longtime housekeeper, made the herbed chicken that afternoon and left foolproof instructions for heating it up. We are in the kitchen and dining area of his loft, a vast and monumentally cluttered space on the second floor of an Upper East Side town house that was once a commercial laundry. The legendary Avedon studio is downstairs, the main part of it anyway; additional workspaces for his team of fifteen associates have taken root on the two floors above his living quarters. Your first impression here is that there’s too much of everything. There are seventeen different-size lighted candles on the long dining table, and bowls of blueberries and blackberries and nuts and cheeses, and photographs both framed and unframed, and pots of narcissus and orchids, and an out-of-control bamboo tree that brushes the ceiling, and a bright red leather boxing glove that’s just arrived from Paris. (“Since this was a rough week for me, a French friend sent it over.”)

Avedon is in constant motion, checking the oven, darting here and there, running his fingers through his long silver-white hair, reaching under his glasses to rub his eyes. A lithe, compact bundle of nervous energy, he is wearing blue jeans, loafers without socks, and a blue shirt with ASTAIRE LIVES printed on the pocket; he had it put there because this was the shirt he was wearing when he heard that Fred Astaire, his childhood idol, had just died. With Avedon, conversation doesn’t just flow—it runs and jumps and turns on a dime and sometimes goes in two or more directions at once. In the fifteen minutes before dinner is ready, he covers the origins of his three favorite chicken recipes (Janet Cam’s Buddhist Chicken, Marcella Hazan’s Chicken with Three Lemons, and Verlie’s own Herbed Chicken); Chekhov’s short stories— “Did you know that he wrote 300? I’ve ordered the whole thirteen-volume set”; his son John’s work as a foreign relations adviser to and biographer of the Dalai Lama of Tibet; the young boxer in Phoenix, whom he photographed for The New Yorker yesterday; the three negative reviews of An Autobiography in The New York Times, which should have killed sales of the $100 book but didn’t; and the critical knives that are being whetted for his Whitney show, which was viciously attacked by Hilton Kramer in The New York Observer two years in advance of its opening. (“This is the ultimate capitulation to celebrity, money and fashion at the expense of art.”) “Reviews no longer victimize me,” Avedon says. “Or define me, or elate me, or stop me from working.”

In The New York Times Book Review, Maud Lavin wrote, “Mr. Avedon’s close, hard stare, his emptied backgrounds and his graphically spectacular compositions do not tell us any more about the social context of napalm victims than they do about fashion models. These techniques do not unmask the ambiguities of people’s lives. What they demonstrate is the extraordinary high degree of control Mr. Avedon exerts in all his confrontations with his subjects.” In the daily Times, Margo Jefferson said of the portraits in Avedon’s book, “By the end, I was rooting for anyone who managed to escape with a shred of self-determination intact.” Andy Grundberg’s more recent notice in the Book Review said that An Autobiography showed Avedon “at his most characteristic: controlling of his subjects and manipulative of his audience, driven to redeem himself from the taint of commerce, obsessed with the judgments of a disembodied posterity.”

Why does Avedon get attacked so savagely? His tremendous success as a fashion photographer is one obvious reason: How dare he presume to be an artist as well? Avedon has fought this dichotomy all his professional life, insisting that there is no difference between his fashion work, his reportage, and the body of portraiture that is his principal claim to recognition as an artist. “I think art history will see him as one of the great portraitists of the twentieth century,” says David Ross, the Whitney’s director, who has come in for a lot of abuse himself over his decision to present an Avedon retrospective. “He’s spent so much of his life in analysis, and in the quest of understanding who he is—this tortured, self-driven Jewish man who is trying to understand himself by looking at other people and their lives, and looking at the way things work, and trying to see into that borderline area between madness and beauty and power and powerlessness. He’s looked hard, as all great artists do.”

Ross insists that working with Avedon on the Whitney retrospective did not involve pitched battles over who was in control. “When we started working on this show, I said to Dick, ‘This is the show that needs to be done for you, not by you; you need to have that happen, as every artist does.’ On the design level, Dick was as directorial as ever. You would have to be a complete fool not to make use of Dick and Mary Shanahan, an amazing designer who works with him. But on a curatorial level, he really let Jane Livingston choose the show. The primary selection of pictures, the primary story that’s being told in the show and in the catalog, is Jane’s.”

The oven timer announces that the chicken is ready. He carves it deftly, serves it with his special house salad—tiny mâche lettuce leaves and shaved Parmesan. The bread is folded into the napkins to keep it fresh. The wine is a 1987 Margaux. The plates are oversize Italian faience from Siena, boldly colorful against the deep blue tablecloth. “You mustn’t think that I care about candle colors and tablecloths and stuff like that,” he says. He does care, nevertheless. It’s all part of the Avedon performance, a never-ending engagement with the visual world in all its forms.

Is it unfair to say that Avedon’s portraits are manipulative, overly controlled, and “trapped in narcissism,” as Maud Lavin charged in The New York Times? This criticism is often heard, and to some extent it may be justified. But then, all great portraits are in a sense self-portraits, and all artists exercise manipulation and control. When Avedon takes a portrait, it is the record of an intense, indelibly personal encounter between the photographer and the subject, whether the subject happens to be a fashion model or a drifter, an actor or a napalm victim, ex-president Dwight David Eisenhower or Jacob Israel Avedon, the photographer’s 87-year-old father, dying of cancer. And if there is sometimes more of Richard Avedon than of the subject in this encounter, well, that’s all in the nature of the performance that Avedon demands in his life and work. But what if the subject won’t perform? Doesn’t this happen in his current avatar as The New Yorker’s staff photographer? “Oh, yes,” he says. “Of course. I’m about as interested in David Dinkins and Rudy Giuliani . . . but that’s part of the job. I’m quite willing to do photographs that are not pure expressions of myself, like the one of Steve Martin on the wall here. He was enormously generous in the sitting, but there’s no such thing as cutting through to Steve Martin. Steve Martin uses his comic genius like a wall. There’s no penetrating it, and I respect that.” Later, he shows me the note Steve Martin sent him after the sitting: "Dear Richard, Yours was the first photo shoot I ever enjoyed . . . . I hope we can become very close friends forsaking all others and have lunches and dinners together six days a week.”

David Ross told me a story about watching Avedon at work on his photographic series called In the American West. “One of the great emblematic West pictures is of a guy with his shirt half over his shoulders. He has a kind of S-shaped body. I remember seeing that guy on the midway of a state fair in southern Colorado. He was the kind of guy I would have crossed the street to avoid. He was tough, and angry, and on the line of being psychotic, and all my good Jewish radar tells me stay away, no eye contact, keep moving. But Dick goes right up and starts talking to him, and within five minutes he is pouring his energy out for Dick in front of a white drop cloth tacked up on a side of a shed. It was astounding to see how he communicates and puts people at ease and allows them to come through.”

Dick is slightly displeased with himself over the chicken. “A little dry, don’t you think? It’s so nice when it’s really juicy. I think we didn’t need that last fifteen minutes.” He has another helping anyway. And he orders me to strip my wishbone clean so he can hang it on the lip of a special pitcher that holds ten or twelve others. “I still have wishes,” he says. “Being 70 doesn’t preclude that.” Dinner consists of one main course plus dessert, simple but extravagant. Another time, you might have a baked potato smothered in beluga caviar, or the special borscht that he carried home in a cardboard container one night from a Russian restaurant in Brighton Beach—he enriches it with piroshki. If he’s serving pasta, it will be Cipriani’s, or else mushroom pasta by his friend China Machado, who was once one of his models and now has a store in Water Mill. Long Island. He jumps up and brings over a box of the Cipriani pasta from the open larder shelves on which are stacked sixteen others. “Just try one of these,” he says of the Cipriani masterpiece. “It takes about a minute and a half to cook. It’s all egg.”

A few days earlier, he had told me that I didn’t have an “Avedon face.” I ask him what he means by an Avedon face. “It’s very varied,” he says. “One of the great Avedon faces is Michelangelo Antonioni’s. There are artists just as complicated as Antonioni, but their complexity isn’t available to my camera. Fellini’s was not an Avedon face. Roy Lichtenstein’s is. I can’t explain it exactly. It’s not about being ravaged or flawed. It’s about contradictions, dialogue, arguments. The soul’s confusion on the face.”

Even in his fashion work he captured that confusion, as Penelope Tree attested in a letter to Avedon about her portrait in An Autobiography. “Of course I identified with being caged, isolated, and utterly bewildered, but I thought I was doing a better job of hiding it! Trust you to see right through. I guess you always did.”

The encounter between Avedon and subject is what makes the portrait, and that usually has a lot to do with what Avedon is feeling at the moment he takes the photograph. Does this make him a monster egoist, as some of his critics maintain? Or is he simply doing what Titian, Velázquez, Francis Bacon, or any great artist does? “Of course, of course,” he says. “Art isn’t art because someone uses a paintbrush. Photography is either good or bad, and when it’s good it’s like any art that’s good. It becomes Art.

“What the subject brings to the camera and what I do with that is what makes the photograph. In photographing my father,” he says, referring to the famous series of his father dying, “I was looking at him. and he was looking at me. The last thing he saw as he was dying was his son. It’s clear to me that he became, in that moment, in that image, what he saw. And what he saw was me.”

Avedon had his own portrait taken for this article. He chose the photographer: his great contemporary and rival, Irving Penn. On the day of the sitting. Avedon had the flu and such severe stomach pains that he called his doctor, from Penn’s studio, for a prescription. “Will I be loopy if I take it?” he asked. “I have an interview with the London Times right after this, and then I’m flying to Hyannis Port to photograph Ethel Kennedy.” “No loopier than usual” was the doctor’s reply. Avedon had brought along a legendary coat from the fifties to be photographed in, a heavy old shearling that he had won in a bet with the model Suzy Parker; it had once warmed Marilyn Monroe, and Isabelle Adjani had worn it in an Avedon photograph. Penn took some shots of him in the coat, but the image that won out shows him in an open-collared work shirt, looking haunted and strangely romantic. “He has a drama that we got that I don’t associate with him,” Penn said afterward. “Like something out of the French Revolution.”

Although Avedon had been photographed twice before by Penn, he tells me that this was the first time he had felt “ready” for the experience. “It’s a wonderful picture,” he says, “the only real portrait of me by Penn. Maybe by anybody. He’s caught something. The real strength of any portrait is to go beneath the surface and into the contradictions within the life. And he’s done that so completely in this portrait. It’s about a kind of crumbling part of me that’s a cross between arrogance and suspicion. Penn’s portrait has nothing to do with looking good, and in this case, it has very little to do with composition. It has a rawness—I mean, it’s more of an Avedon than a Penn. Ha! And yet it could never have been taken by anyone but Penn.”

What is the difference between an Avedon portrait and a Penn portrait?

“I think Penn’s great strength lies in his power of composition and in the very still moment that reveals. From the beginning, I’ve felt that any composition that is visible in my photographs takes you away from the direct confrontation that I look for. If anyone said of a picture of mine. ‘Look at the composition in that,’ I’d be embarrassed. I’d know that I failed.

“Rivalry is a funny word to use about Penn and me. It doesn’t cover or even hint at the relationship. In the years when I was at Harper’s Bazaar [ 1945 to 1965] and he was at Vogue, and we were both covering the same celebrities, I watched every move he made, and I think in some way it helped define me. I was always excited by Penn, in awe of Penn, and wanted to top him or equal him, or be the opposite of him. I think of him as a classicist and of me as an eclectic. I was fired by him. inspired by him. pushed by his standards, his rigor, his excellence.”

I ask him which other photographers he has admired. “Certainly Diane Arbus, Julia Margaret Cameron in the old days. But Cartier-Bresson rules. Walker Evans is a miniaturist compared to him. There are wonderful photographers—Robert Frank, for example—who have mastered small areas of the territory Cartier-Bresson laid out. The world of photojournalism is littered with Bresson babies. He is the photographic Tolstoy of the twentieth century.

“Helmut Newton redefined what a fashion photograph could be. He’s the leader of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. He released everything. He changed what a fashion model could look like and played with vulgarity in a really witty way. After Helmut Newton, you can’t do a certain kind of picture anymore.”

“It’s done all the time, and it’s boring! But when Helmut does it, the erotic focus shifts from the ankle and the smile to the inner thigh.”

It’s a little odd to hear Richard Avedor speak of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. Bruce Weber, one of today’s top fashion photographers who photographed Avedon for this article, sees his influence as being very much alive and in the present. “Richard Avedon is like this wonderful kid you meet at school, who has more energy than anybody else,” Weber says. “He really is open, he engages you in what’s going on in his life, and he makes you then think about your own. He’s influenced a whole generation of photographers who are working now, me included, in that just simply and purely you want to take photographs and to photograph your own life at the same time. Dick’s work is not about fame. It’s really about still being a kid and not being afraid to shoe it.”

We’re heavily into dessert by this time. Dick always serves at least five—three different ice and an orange cake from Sant Ambroeus, fresh blackberries and raspberries, macaroons from Bonté, and a split of the Billecart-Salmon champagne that he discovered years ago at Chez Panisse. He promises next time to make Mike Nichols’s Peach Orgasm (six fresh peaches, two bananas, one and a half cups of sugar, two cups of sour cream, and the juice of one lemon: blend in blender, then put in ice cream maker). He has a file of recipes that he’s picked up from restaurants and friends in various parts of the world. It’s more than enough for a book, but it will have to wait until he’s finished the ten books he’s already under contract to do for Random House: several more collections of his photographs: four teaching books based on his master classes in fashion photography, reportage, portraiture, and the snapshot; and an autobiographical novel that he says he’ll be working on for the rest of his life.

There’s another kind of autobiography on the walls. Hundreds of photographs, clippings, postcards, notes, mementos, and reproductions of famous paintings are pinned to the soft beaverboard, some of them yellow with age. Shots of Fred Astaire dancing, and one of Astaire with the young Avedon during the filming of Funny Face, in which the great dancer played the part of a fashion photographer based on Richard Avedon. A more mature Avedon with Audrey Hepburn, Miss Funny Face herself. The New York Post’s front page on Liz Taylor’s eighth marriage, with eight “I Do’s” in bold type. Three Avedon press cards for the year he went to Vietnam. A news photo of an unidentified man frozen to death beneath the ice of a lake in Queens, New York. Athletes in violent action. Snapshots of Evelyn, his wife, whom he hasn’t lived with for many years (he still sees her for dinner or a movie at least once a week), and one of their son, John, and John’s wife, Maura Moynihan, the senator’s daughter, with their son, Michael. A blown-up page of The New York Times Magazine with head shots of seventeen people whom Stalin had killed. (“They were photographed and then they were killed,” Avedon says. “Look, aren’t these the most pure and perfect portraits?”) A life-size blowup of Ruby Holden, the Nevada pawnbroker whom Avedon photographed in 1980. A poster of Goya’s Contessa Chinchón, which he considers one of the great portraits in Western art—”an infantile woman in an evening gown,” he says. “A combination of fashion and portraiture. Most portraiture involves fashion. That’s what Penn does. That’s what I try to do.”

Fashion photographs, by Avedon or anyone else, are nonetheless conspicuously absent from this wall of memories and momentary enthusiasms. No Dovima with elephants, no Suzy Parker, no Twiggy, no Jean Shrimpton or Stephanie Seymour, his current favorite. Other than a few isolated examples, only one room (out of fifteen) at the Whitney retrospective will be devoted to Avedon’s fashion work, and this makes you wonder about his reiterated argument that all his work, fashion included, is a part of the same seamless web. Avedon’s ambivalent relationship with the world of high fashion, which has given him the means to pursue his ambitions as an artist, was exacerbated in 1988 when he had a falling out with Vogue’s new editor. He had photographed almost every Vogue cover since 1966 but found he disagreed with Anna Wintour about how Vogue covers should look, and she stopped using him for covers. Recently, on the occasion of this interview, he wrote Wintour a letter and signed it “Let’s bury the lipsticks. Dick.” In the meanwhile, he has not lacked for commercial outlets. Tomorrow he starts a big job for Versace—racks of dresses and underwear and tables of accessories have taken over the far end of the long room, for a weeklong shoot that will be the firm’s next major ad campaign.

The problem is he won’t be using Stephanie Seymour, who is pregnant. “I’ll never forgive her,” he says, mock-seriously. Avedon has always liked to work more or less exclusively with one model at a time. Suzy Parker, his favorite of the fifties, has vivid memories of their working relationship. “We had become so attuned to each other,” she tells me. “First of all, we shared an outrageous sense of humor. Second, we worked to music, so we were already into movement. I mean, I was never still. Before Dick, modeling was like being crucified most of the time. They’d have tissue paper stuffed up your dress, they’d have clothespins and safety pins up and down your back. They’d have strings that wouldn’t show to hold the movement of the skirt. The whole thing was absolutely ghastly. With Dick it was always movement. And I was young enough to walk out on one of the gargoyle heads of Nôtre Dame. Nobody else would do that. I was young enough to go out on high heels on one of those beams of the Eiffel Tower. I did roller-skating on cobblestones. He would set up these crazy situations.” Penelope Tree, one of his favorites in the sixties, says that “when you worked with Dick, you were so caught up in the moment, some intensely personal sort of moment. I’ve never had that experience with any other photographer before or since. It was really like having a love affair, except it wasn’t at all physical.”

The back wall, behind the Versace paraphernalia, is crowded with images of a different sort. Above low bookshelves filled with art books are framed photographs by Baron de Meyer, Atget, Brassaï, Man Ray, Cameron, and Avedon, most of them of disturbed-looking women. Also an Avedon portrait of his father that was the poster for his 1974 show at the Museum of Modern Art, and one of his horrific images of a grimacing Oscar Levant, which Avedon sometimes considers his finest portrait. The dark side of the Avedon psyche is in command here. (Avedon: “It is through the dark part of the eye that we see light.”) Nearby on the side wall is a huge blowup of four grimy coal miners, from the American West series. “I like that one less and less,” he says. “My hand is just too strong in it. Just too much of me manipulating. The craftsmanship, the composition. It’s all too apparent. It doesn’t reach below the surface.”

He laughs and makes a sweeping gesture that somehow includes the room and everything in it. “You know what I’m going to do? Empty this place out. Put everything on the walls in boxes, or the warehouse or the fire. I’ll just dump everything and start again, see who I become. Try to do it better, more deeply, and if I lose it, hope that my friends shoot me or at least stop me from becoming Steichen, photographing the apple tree outside my window with a new young wife kneeling at my feet.”

There’s a brick fireplace that Avedon never uses because pigeons have nested in the chimney. The mantel is cluttered with stuff, like every other flat surface here. An empty bottle of 1923 Lafite-Rothschild, Avedon’s birth year, stands on a boxed bottle of the same vintage, undrunk, “waiting for the right occasion.” There are also three parcels in brown wrapping paper, tied in ordinary string, unopened. He knows what one of them is—a bleached-white skeleton of a bird’s wing that washed up on the beach of Antigua years ago, during a photographic shoot with Suzy Parker; Dick and Suzy both wanted it, and it became their “bone of contention,” which travels back and forth between them. The other two boxes, he says, “I hope to open just before I die. They’re from someone who means a great deal to me. If I’m alone when I die, opening them—discovering what’s in there—will be like the right person holding my hand.”

It’s a quarter to twelve, way after his bedtime. He wakes up at five every morning, gets out of bed at six, turns the coffee on, and does last night’s dishes “for therapy.” Breakfast is coffee and fresh apple juice, squeezed by Verlie from whole apples the day before. His personal trainer comes three mornings a week at 7:30 to give him a one-hour workout. When he says good night, his voice is a little raspier, but his restless energy shows no signs of flagging.

It’s the next morning, 7:30, and Avedon is calling in great agitation. He says last night’s interview “didn’t work,” and we have to try again. This time he’ll invite his old and close friend Twyla Tharp, and he tells me I can be a fly on the wall while they wing it conversationally. OK, I say, well aware that there’s no arguing with Avedon in his control-freak mood. I go, I listen, I’m charmed, I’m well fed—lamb roast and applesauce with horseradish, homemade pumpkin pie and the usual cornucopia of desserts. His son, John, is there, and John’s nearly three-year-old son, Michael. So are the seventeen candles, which almost send the bamboo tree up in flames. It’s a warm, family sort of evening, and the conversation goes off in two dozen directions, and if it were reproduced here, we could have yet another portrait of Richard Avedon. The possibilities are endless. •

#6574. Seeing Green on the GQ Men of the Year Red Carpet

The carpet at our annual GQ Men of the Year party may be red, but we’re seeing—dare we say it—Brat green.

Last night, as the stars of our latest MOTY issue gathered at the iconic Chateau Marmont, we noticed a verdant trend emerge on the carpet. Who better to kick things off than two of the most boisterous creatives from our 2026 Breakout Stars crew? First up was actor-comedian Stavros Halkias, who sported a screaming lime green suit by Alan David, a matching Cego silk shirt, and olive-hued Bottega Veneta loafers. Not far behind was Club Kid director-star Jordan Firstman, who also greened out in a full runway look from Anthony Vaccarello’s final menswear collection for Saint Laurent: a boxy, greenish khaki suit with bejeweled buttons, layered over a liquid-silk chartreuse shirt. Both ensembles sure were bright, but ask any color theorist and they’ll probably tell you that wearing green on a red carpet is a surefire way to stand out—they’re opposite of each other on the color wheel for a reason!

The chartreuse looks just kept on coming: the one and only Ice Spice donned a flowing green DSquared2 dress, with matching green eyeshadow (and a curiously hirsute handbag) to boot.

Elsewhere on the carpet, The Bear’s Ayo Edebiri—already a bonafide menswear star—opted for a different but equally striking shade of green. Her sleek striped power suit by London-based designer Connor Ives popped thanks to a kelly green shirt and a contrasting crimson tie. (Edebiri wasn’t the only woman who rocked tailoring on the MOTY carpet this year: model Cara Delevingne, who stars in Firstman’s Club Kid, wore a slouchy-chic black suit by Saint Laurent, while Luciana Damon, wife of cover star Matt, layered a tuxedo-style bolero jacket over her gown.)

If the MOTY red carpet can provide any insights into the year of fashion ahead, we’ll surely be seeing even more green in the months to come. We’re manifesting abundance, in more ways than one.

#6573. There's an Advent Calendar for (Almost) Everything

Souped-up Advent calendars are here to stay this holiday season, with just about every big player in food and beverage getting in on the trend.

Experts say there’s a mix of factors at play as for their rise in popularity: little treats and micro indulgences in an expensive world, the idea of “saving big” on high-value bundles, and the sensory satisfaction of unboxing 25(ish) little boxes leading up to Christmas.

“There’s something so special about having a small treat to look forward to each day,” Sockerbit Scandinavian candy founders Florence Baras and Stefan Ernberg said in a statement. Sockerbit is one of several newbies to the food Advent calendar space this year (and one of our new faves).

Advent Center, a hub for data and reviews for thousands of Advent calendars globally, says there are around 250 food and drink calendars on the market this year. The category makes up about a third of the 2026 calendars it lists.

Max Zeshut, Advent Center’s founder, said food and drink calendars work well because they’re a cheaper, noncommittal entry point into the ritual, compared to, for instance, a beauty box. And for all the new and zany iterations out there, chocolate calendars remain an anchor.

Broadly, the global Advent calendar market is anticipated to grow from $1.32 billion in 2024 to $2.47 billion by 2033, according to research compiled by Accio, a B2B platform. Food and drink calendars hold a huge share of that, with the help of mainstays like Bonne Maman, whose annual calendars have inspired “Jamvent” fan groups for a decade, alongside newcomers that announced inaugural calendars this season.

“As a small team, we try to be very conscious of the operational demands of every product launch,” Fishwife CEO and co-founder Becca Millstein told Bon Appétit. “Still, the demand [for calendars] grew too loud to ignore, so we decided to go for it.”

Millstein cited Fishwife’s success in the online gifting space as motivation to launch a calendar this year. Fishwife’s includes 12 doors of tinned fish and extras, retailing for $150. The company said the calendar’s “elements of surprise and delight” drives chatter and user-generated content on social media.

“In the end, we simply had to do it,” Millstein said.

When the Sichuan condiment company Fly By Jing’s Advent calendar launched in 2024, it sold out in about a month. That’s when founder Jing Gao knew the brand was onto something.

Gao said that 65% of its Advent calendars were purchased by new customers this year and that historically, 20% of customers who purchase a calendar go on to make another Fly By Jing purchase by the end of the year.

“To me, that really speaks to the power of discovery and giving people a chance to explore our flavors in a fun, unexpected way,” Gao said. “We never want that sense of discovery to go away, even for people who have been with us from the beginning. It's become such a fun creative outlet for our team. I think that joy really comes through in the experience.”

The stewards at Onyx Coffee Lab in Arkansas describe a similar phenomenon. “There's so much storytelling, education, and human connection surrounding coffee, and Advent gives us a unique opportunity to explore those things in ways that might not make sense within our everyday offerings,” Onyx’s co-founder Andrea Allen said. Their box features 24 different coffees, each a 56-gram package of whole beans that are roasted on a schedule for peak brewing by their respective reveal day.

At Bonne Maman, Advent calendar planning starts two years in advance. The development team pays close attention to seasonal ingredients and market trends to produce 24 limited-edition jams and spreads made just for the calendar. The result sells out every year, with production growing by 400% since 2017, according to a spokesperson. This year will mark 10 years of the Bonne Maman Advent calendar.

“We’re grateful to the fans who have made it part of their holidays,” a company spokesperson said. “On social media, we see everything from matcha pairings and coffee creations to new takes on toast, along with plenty of flavor-by-flavor reviews. Many fans also write to us to tell us which flavor they loved most. It helps us decide which flavors should return or come in larger sizes.”

Have we stretched Advent calendar hype to its absolute limits? Advent Center’s Zeshut says no.

“The clearest sign of demand is that people search for calendars that don't exist,” he said. “There's no official Monster Energy calendar this year, and 'monster Advent calendar' is still one of the most searched terms that brings people to our site,” he said. “I don't think we've reached peak calendar, but we may have reached peak chocolate.”

#6572. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6571. Poulet Basquaise

Rich tomatoes, stewed onions and peppers, and tender bone-in chicken make this Spanish- and French-inspired poulet Basquaise recipe extremely flavorful while still being surprisingly easy to make. Savory and rustic, it’s a stew that’s ideal for making ahead and enjoying all week long. The key ingredient? Piment d’Espelette—the regional spice known for its peppery, smoky essence. If you’re looking to master a classic dish or simply want a reliable, cozy weeknight dinner, then this recipe won’t let you down.

Heat a large skillet with oil and season the chicken with salt. Working in batches, add the chicken pieces and sear until the skin is golden in color, which should take 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the chicken to a heatproof plate.

Then reduce the heat and add the onion, bell peppers, garlic, piment d’Espelette, and salt. You’ll want to stir this once in a while so it doesn’t stick, but also let the vegetables soften. This should take 8 to 10 minutes.

At this point, increase the heat again and add the wine. Scrape up any bits on the bottom and allow those peppers and onions to absorb the wine. The liquid should reduce.

Add the tomatoes and broth and bring to a simmer. Be careful of splattering sauce and adjust the heat as needed. Place the chicken back into the skillet, skin side up, and cook until the chicken is tender and nearly falling off the bone. The sauce should also be thicker and fragrant. This should take about 30 to 40 minutes.

Stir in the chorizo and cook until it’s warmed through. Top it off with thyme and serve!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. It’s certainly a great meal-prep dish. Make this on a Sunday night for lunch Monday and Tuesday.

#6569. 37 Family Dinner Ideas You’ll Make on Repeat

The good news about “family-friendly” dinners? They can be whatever you want them to be. Loaded sweet potato wedges eaten straight from the sheet pan? Absolutely. A dose of nostalgia by way of movie-night sloppy Joes, updated with a fiery kick of gochujang? No question about it. These are dinners for cautious eaters and adventurous ones alike—some familiar, some a little unexpected, and all worth bringing to the table.

Whether tonight calls for a cozy soup (that you can set and forget in your Instant Pot) or easy fish tacos (we have a hunch they’ll become part of your regular weeknight dinner rotation), we’ve got plenty of ideas to keep dinner interesting all year long.

Set tortillas, flaky cod or halibut, spicy lime sauce, and toppings out family-style and let everyone assemble their own piled-high tacos. It’s a simple weeknight family dinner that doubles as a choose-your-own-adventure activity.

Packed with ground chicken, white beans, and canned green chiles, this fast-cooking stew only gets better over time, so make a big batch. We promise, you won’t mind eating it two days in a row.

High-protein cottage cheese replaces often-pricier ricotta in this thrifty-ish spin on a familiar family favorite. More shocking: mozzarella is out too, in favor of tangy super-melter Fontina.

If your family loves pepperoni pizza, they’ll love this baked pasta, which hits all the saucy, spicy, cheesy notes with no takeout required. Roasting the sauce on a sheet pan concentrates its flavor before everything gets a blanket of cheese.

All the appeal of a spicy salmon roll, reassembled as a family-friendly bowl. Pickled cucumber and spicy mayo accompany crackly, broiled salmon cubes for a dinner that’s as fun to eat as it is easy to customize.

Smoky-sweet Korean gochujang lends a hum of heat to this riff on a childhood favorite. Soft buns and a stack of napkins do the rest.

Think chicken pot pie, but in cozy soup form. Complete with crackly, buttery shards of puff pastry you can tear and share, this family meal practically demands a crowd around the table.

This shareable skillet is packed with the flavors of a family-favorite appetizer, with roasted poblanos, red onions, and jalapeños smothered in cheesy sauce.

Store-bought pizza dough makes this family-friendly dinner a snap, even on busy weeknights. This California Pizza Kitchen-inspired recipe is smoky-sweet thanks to barbecue sauce, Gouda cheese, and frizzled mushrooms.

Store-bought zhug, a Yemeni-spiced cilantro sauce, and your broiler are the shortcuts to juicy, charred, baked chicken without a grill. It’s an easy, low-fuss dinner that delivers big flavor.

Somewhere between nachos and loaded potatoes, roasted sweet potatoes get topped with spiced ground beef and briny kimchi for a main dish that’s complete enough to enjoy straight off the sheet pan.

Genuinely juicy, supremely crispy, flavored like falafel, and browned in a skillet for ultimate ease. Serve them with your favorite burger toppings for an easy family dinner.

Sometimes you just want to cook an old faithful—the kind of dinner you know the whole family will love. That’s when you reach for this rich, cheesy, ever-reliable baked ziti.

These vibrant (and vegetarian) kale-and-black-bean-stuffed peppers are a repeat-worthy, one-dish dinner full of hearty flavor. Stirring a dollop of sour cream into the tomato sauce gives it rich texture.

Everyone loves a customizable dinner, and this shawarma-spiced chicken is made for it. Set out warm pitas and all your favorite fixings, like sliced tomatoes and cucumber spears, and let everyone build their perfect plate.

Shrimp cooked in garlicky, lemony butter is bound to be delicious. Serve it with crusty bread or toss it with pasta for a cozy weeknight meal the whole family will love.

Golden-edged tofu meets a bold, spicy satay-inspired peanut sauce in this quick, satisfying dish. Pile it over rice or serve with naan for scooping.

Canned pumpkin is good for way more than sweets. Here, lemon, Parmesan, and chile flakes turn it into a creamy, savory sauce that comes together while the pasta boils.

Spinach-packed dal is a lifesaver on nights when you’re strapped for time but craving something deeply comforting. Serve it with rice or flatbread for a quick vegetarian meal.

Tender soy-glazed chicken meatballs and crisp sesame green beans make a balanced family dinner that needs little else than a pot of rice.

Transform two favorite store-bought ingredients—cheese ravioli and crispy fried onions—into a rich and luscious skillet dinner with a crispy, savory top.

This sunny, dressed-for-summer family dinner relies on a pantry-friendly chicken marinade. All you need: sugar, vinegar, salt, and a few spices. Add couscous and dinner is done.

Make these succulent pork chops when it’s 6:26 p.m. on a Monday and you haven’t figured out what’s for dinner. The sweet-and-savory sauce makes this quick weeknight meal feel planned ahead.

Canned chickpeas and frozen broccoli keep this one-skillet dinner fast and thrifty, while cream cheese delivers on the faux pasta Alfredo front.

Leftover rice meets plenty of fresh ginger, soy sauce, and eggs in this satisfying 20-minute dinner. The key is starting with cold, cooked rice, which crisps up beautifully in a hot skillet.

Cherry tomatoes burst around a block of feta in the oven, forming a tangy, creamy pasta sauce. Calabrian chile paste brings a welcome kick that cuts through the richness.

This hearty catch-all skillet dinner tastes just as good in egg burritos the next morning, or make and freeze it up to three months ahead.

Upgrade grilled salmon with a punchy, vibrant dill chimichurri. It’s quick, fresh, and feels fancy enough to make you feel like you have your life together.

Much faster to make than risotto, this lemony, bright orzotto gets its herby savoriness from a pantry savior: store-bought jarred pesto.

Your favorite party dip, now in pasta form. Frozen spinach and jarred artichokes keep things convenient, while plenty of bubbling cheese makes this skillet dinner every bit as comforting as the original.

So tired you’re considering takeout? Try this simple, speedy stir-fry instead—it comes together in 25 minutes but tastes restaurant-quality.

Store-bought gnocchi bakes up crispy on the outside and pillowy on the inside, the perfect complement to browned spicy sausage and a sprinkle of finely grated Parmesan.

Give mac and cheese the hot wing treatment, because sometimes one comfort food just isn’t enough. It’s creamy, tangy, and just spicy enough to keep you coming back for another forkful.

Let your Instant Pot handle this warm, spicy, protein-packed, family-friendly dinner idea. Top it with a dollop of sour cream, a sprinkle of pickled onions, and whatever else floats your fancy.

Chicken and cabbage may sound pretty basic, but this stir-fry is anything but. Sambal oelek and fish sauce give it plenty of spicy, salty flavor, making it a nutritious family dinner that packs a punch.

Crisp bibb lettuce leaves make the perfect cups for this spicy larb-inspired chicken, which you can dress up with fresh herbs and fried shallots. It’s a fun, hands-on family dinner that gets everyone involved.

This is the kind of salad that can hold its own as a family dinner, packed with roasted sweet potato and tofu, crisp red apple, and a bright, herby green goddess dressing.

#6568. The Best Dressed Stars of the Week Proved Formal Can Be Fun

Starting now, the season of never-ending holiday parties begins—and if one is in need of dressing inspiration, some recent red carpet moments had plenty to offer. The best dressed stars of the week were those who leaned into glamorous fun and really went for it. Formal looks were accentuated with bright colors and saucy little ties, which made everything feel vibrant and not-so-stuffy. It’s a perfect mood to embrace for the festive holiday schedule ahead.

Take Ayo Edebiri at the GQ Men of the Year Awards in L.A. this weekend. The actor chose a pinstriped Connor Ives suit, but amped it up with a minty shirt and elongated red tie. Imagine wearing that to your office party: you’d be the talk of the water cooler for weeks! Another sleek two-piece moment came courtesy of Zoe Kravitz, at the premiere of How to Rob a Bank. The star chose a golden Saint Laurent crop top and trouser set, putting a sexier new twist on holiday metallics.

#6567. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)
